figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Codebase-Memory architecture. Source files are parsed via Tree-Sitter, stored as a knowledge graph in SQLite, and exposed to LLM agents through 14 typed MCP tools. A file watcher triggers incremental re-indexing on changes.
figures.headline: The architecture stores parsed source in a SQLite graph that a file watcher keeps current for 14 MCP tools.

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) coding agents typically explore codebases through repeated file-reading and grep-searching, consuming thousands of tokens per query without structural understanding. We present Codebase-Memory, an open-source system that constructs a persistent, Tree-Sitter-based knowledge graph via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), parsing 66 languages through a multi-phase pipeline with parallel worker pools, call-graph traversal, impact analysis, and community discovery [1]. Evaluated across 31 real-world repositories, Codebase-Memory achieves 83% answer quality versus 92% for a file-exploration agent, at ten times fewer tokens and 2.1 times fewer tool calls. For graph-native queries such as hub detection and caller ranking, it matches or exceeds the explorer on 19 of 31 languages.

sections.body: The paper argues that coding agents explore codebases through repeated file reads and grep searches, which costs many tokens and tool calls. It proposes a persistent knowledge graph built with Tree-Sitter, stored in SQLite and exposed through MCP as 14 typed structural tools. The system covers 66 languages and includes 6-strategy call resolution, Louvain community detection, and incremental re-indexing. The contributions are the graph architecture, the MCP tool interface, and a head-to-head evaluation across 31 languages. That evaluation reports 83% answer quality against 92% for a file-exploration agent, with fewer tokens and tool calls.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Text-based code exploration by coding agents scales poorly, so the paper proposes a queryable code knowledge graph exposed via MCP.

sections.body: The related work covers structural code analysis, including Program Dependence Graphs, Code Property Graphs and CodeQL, which the authors describe as heavyweight and not designed for LLM consumption. It then reviews code retrieval systems that build code graphs for LLMs, such as KGCompass at 58.3% on SWE-bench Lite and RepoGraph with a 32.8% relative improvement on SWE-bench. Graph-guided agent navigation work such as LocAgent is also covered. The authors position their work as orthogonal to agent-strategy research: they optimize the retrieval layer, which can combine with any of these agent architectures. Token-efficiency methods such as LLMLingua form a separate line.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work builds heavyweight code graphs or improves agent strategy, leaving the retrieval layer largely unchanged.

sections.body: The Parse stage extracts definitions, call sites, imports and references from Tree-Sitter ASTs for 66 languages, with LSP-style type resolution for Go, C and C++. A multi-phase pipeline with parallel worker pools flushes the graph to SQLite. Call resolution uses a 6-strategy cascade with confidence scores from 0.95 down to 0.30–0.40. Community detection applies Louvain modularity optimization to the call graph. A file watcher uses XXH3 content hashes to re-index only changed files. The system ships as one statically linked binary. The security section describes an 8-layer CI audit suite, release verification steps and code-level protections, including a SQLite authorizer that blocks ATTACH and DETACH.
sections.heading: System Design
sections.headline: Codebase-Memory parses 66 languages into one SQLite knowledge graph and serves it through 14 MCP tools.

sections.body: The head-to-head benchmark has 12 question categories across 31 languages, each tested on a real repository from 78 nodes (HCL/Terraform) to 49,398 nodes (Python/Django). The MCP Agent and an Explorer Agent both used Claude Opus 4.6 and were graded by the first author against reference answers. The MCP Agent averaged 2.3 tool calls per question against 4.8, and ~1,000 tokens per question against ~10,000. It matched or exceeded the explorer on hub detection and caller ranking in 19 of 31 languages. The explorer kept an advantage for full source context in 16 of 31 languages. Macro-heavy C scored 0.58 against 1.00. Indexing the Django repository took ~6 s.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: On 31 languages the MCP agent scored 0.83 against 0.92 for the explorer while using 2.1 times fewer tool calls.

sections.body: The discussion separates graph from text retrieval: the MCP agent wins on cross-file structural queries, while the explorer keeps an advantage for full source context and exhaustive pattern matching. The authors suggest a hybrid design with file-exploration fallback for source-level tasks. The discussion also argues for supply-chain verification of MCP servers. The threats to validity state one LLM backend, Claude Opus 4.6, and one repository per language. They also note the static-only graph, which omits runtime behavior and dynamic dispatch, and a default ceiling of 100,000 rows in `query_graph`. All performance measurements come from one Apple M3 Pro.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Structure helps cross-file queries, but results come from one backend and one repository per language.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the main claim: treating code structure as a queryable graph gives order-of-magnitude efficiency gains with competitive accuracy. It cites the Tree-Sitter pipeline, 6-strategy call resolution and Louvain community detection, with queries running in under a millisecond. It notes that the single C binary with zero dependencies scales to the Linux kernel, with 2.1 M nodes in ~3 minutes. It reports ten times lower token cost and 2.1 times fewer tool calls across 31 languages. It also cites the automated release verification pipeline and early community adoption.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion argues structural retrieval is a viable foundation for LLM-based code intelligence.

sections.body: The Data Availability Statement says the Codebase-Memory source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are publicly available in the project's GitHub repository. The repository is distributed under the MIT license. The version evaluated in this paper corresponds to release v0.5.5, so the reported results can be tied to that specific release. The statement names no other location for the data and describes no further data beyond the source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data it lists.
sections.heading: Data Availability Statement
sections.headline: The source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are public for the evaluated release v0.5.5.
